name: Plantar Heel Pain (Plantar Fasciopathy)
summary: Load-related plantar-medial heel pain, often worst with first steps after rest; the term fasciopathy better reflects many persistent cases.

looksLike: Pain after prolonged standing or walking
redFlags: Night/rest pain, systemic symptoms or malignancy history
Acute trauma with inability to weight bear
firstSteps: Use supportive footwear and temporary taping/heel support if helpful
Begin plantar fascia-specific and calf stretching if tolerated
selfCare: Avoid sudden spikes in standing/running load
Use supportive footwear if it clearly reduces symptoms
Perform daily mobility and progressive strengthening

assess: Pain with windlass loading in some cases

tests.name: Windlass Test
tests.purpose: Load plantar fascia through great-toe extension and assess familiar heel pain.

stages.label: Protection, Education & Symptom-Guided Loading
stages.goal: Address safety, settle excessive irritability and maintain useful movement.
do: Use supportive footwear and temporary taping/heel support if helpful
Begin plantar fascia-specific and calf stretching if tolerated
dose: Plantar fascia-specific stretch: 10-second holds x 10, before first steps and as needed
Calf stretch: 3 x 20–30 seconds if comfortable
moveOn: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.

stages.label: Mobility, Strength & Capacity
stages.goal: Restore the specific strength, mobility and control required by the condition.
when: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.
do: Progress calf and intrinsic foot strengthening
Add progressive resistance rather than relying on stretching alone
moveOn: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.

stages.label: Functional Restoration & Return to Activity
stages.goal: Rebuild real-world, occupational or sporting capacity.
when: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.
do: Return to longer walks, running and occupational standing
dose: Loaded calf raise and hopping: 2–4 sets, graded by tolerance
moveOn: Full task exposure is completed progressively.
No clinically meaningful deterioration during the following 24 hours.

returnCriteria: Repeated calf raises and impact tasks tolerated

logic: Treat the foot and calf as a load-tolerance system rather than assuming a fixed 'spur' is the cause.
First-step pain and cumulative standing/running load are useful markers.
Strength and sensible load management usually matter more than passive treatment.
structures: Plantar aponeurosis, especially medial calcaneal attachment
Intrinsic foot muscles and calf complex influence load capacity
mechanism: Abrupt increase in standing, walking or running
classification: Acute or persistent plantar heel pain
Consider nerve entrapment, stress injury and systemic causes
investigations: Usually clinical; imaging if atypical, trauma, suspected stress fracture or persistent unexplained symptoms.
Consider systemic assessment for bilateral enthesitis with inflammatory features.
manual: Manual therapy may address ankle/foot mobility restrictions short term.
Avoid painful aggressive fascia scraping; combine with loading and education.
Ankle/foot mobilization when a relevant mobility deficit exists
Ankle/foot mobilization can be used when a mobility deficit is clearly relevant.
Soft-tissue work to calf/plantar tissues can be used briefly for symptom relief.
Reassess walking or first-step simulation after treatment.
modalities: Taping or prefabricated orthoses may help short term in selected patients.
Night splints may help persistent first-step pain; shockwave may be considered by a qualified clinician for persistent cases.
Ice massage for comfort if preferred
Taping can provide short-term symptom relief
Passive electrotherapy is not the main treatment
Ice massage 5–10 minutes may be used for comfort.
Taping can be used short term to reduce pain during walking.
dosing: Plantar fascia stretch: 20–30 seconds × 3–5 repetitions, especially before first steps.
Calf stretch: 30 seconds × 3 reps if dorsiflexion is limited.
Calf raises: 3 sets × 8–15 reps, progressing to single leg and added load.
Intrinsic foot exercise: 2–3 sets × 10–15 controlled reps.
progression: Increase calf load and single-leg capacity
Add hopping/running only after daily walking is well tolerated
Progress calf load and walking volume gradually.
Add hopping/running only after daily walking is well tolerated.
Use symptom response the next morning as a useful load marker.
mistakes: Calling every heel pain plantar fasciitis
Focusing only on a heel spur.
Using painful deep massage every day.
pearls: A multimodal plan combining education, stretching and progressive resistance is more useful than one passive modality.
Bilateral heel enthesitis plus inflammatory symptoms warrants broader screening.
education: Explain that the plantar fascia is load-sensitive and often improves with gradual capacity building.
Footwear may help symptoms but is not the only treatment.
escalation: Medical review for suspected stress fracture, persistent severe symptoms or atypical neurological/systemic findings

tests.name: Windlass Test
tests.purpose: Load plantar fascia through great-toe extension and assess familiar heel pain.
tests.patientPosition: Seated or standing; passively extend great toe at MTP joint while observing arch.
tests.therapistPosition: Position yourself to observe and stabilise the relevant segment without forcing the movement.
tests.handPlacement: Use comfortable, controlled contact appropriate to the test; avoid painful compression or excessive force.
procedure: Explain the test and obtain consent.
Screen contraindications and compare sides when appropriate.
Perform the movement slowly and apply only the required resistance or stress.
Record familiar symptom reproduction, range, strength and side-to-side difference.
tests.interpretation: A negative test does not exclude plantar fasciopathy; integrate first-step symptoms and palpation.
tests.clinicalNote: A special test modifies clinical probability; it does not confirm a diagnosis in isolation.
